m.s: The Proclamation of Elizabeth I in 1558
o: Eternal God and King of all kings, I give You thanks for this morning. I rise knowing that the day does not begin with me, but with You, for You kept watch while I slept. Thank You for life, for the health I have, for the home where I rested and for the people You placed at my side. Today I want to begin by acknowledging that You hold time in Your hands and that You govern all that exists.

Lord, sometimes the future seems uncertain to me and what is beyond my control worries me. Governments change, the news frightens and my own plans get bent out of shape. Teach me to believe that the hearts of rulers are in Your hands and that Your purposes endure. I pray for the authorities of my country and of all countries: give them wisdom, justice and fear of You. And for myself, deliver me from anxiety and give me peace.

Guide my decisions today. May my plans submit to Your counsel, may my words be kind and may my work honor Your name. Take care of my family, console those who suffer and strengthen those who feel alone. At the close of the day, may I look back and see Your hand at every step. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 17, 1558, Queen Mary I of England died at St James's Palace in London, and her half-sister Elizabeth was proclaimed queen that same day. The news arrived in a kingdom weary from years of religious tension, fear and uncertainty. Elizabeth was at that time at Hatfield, and the change of reign took place within a few hours.

According to accounts of the time, Parliament met that same morning and decided that Elizabeth would be proclaimed successor immediately. Her adviser, William Cecil, had prepared the text of the proclamation, and everything was done in an orderly way. Elizabeth would govern England for forty-five years, until 1603, and her reign deeply marked the life of the country and its Church. It was a swift and calm change.

What happened that day is a great lesson for faith. Kings come and go, kingdoms change hands and a people's circumstances can shift in a single morning. No one in England knew for certain what was to come. Yet Scripture teaches that the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, who turns it wherever he will. Thrones are temporary; the kingdom of God has no end.

For the believers of that time, and for us today, the message is one of trust. When the future seems uncertain, God has not lost control. He governs the nations, listens to the prayers of his people and fulfills his purposes in his own time. That is why we can pray for our authorities with calm and rest in the fact that our lives are in the hands of the King of kings.
m.c: Go out into your day with the certainty that the Lord holds in his hands both the great affairs and the small details of your life. Do not run ahead of what has not yet come; take each step in faith. May his peace and favor surround you from dawn.
m: There are days when everything seems to shift beneath our feet. Work changes, health changes, the family's situation changes, and we wonder who is in control. The story of this November 17, 1558 reminds us that even the greatest changes in a nation take place under God's gaze. What was a surprise to men was never a mystery to him.

The book of Proverbs says that the king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD, who turns it wherever he will. It also says that many are the plans in the human heart, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand. This does not mean we should not make plans, but that we should make them with humility, knowing that the last word belongs to God and that his purpose is good.

Here is a practical application for today. Write on a piece of paper a situation that worries you and does not depend on you: another person's decision, a piece of news, a result you are waiting for. Present it to God in prayer and say: “Lord, you are in control; I do my part.” Then spend a few minutes praying for your authorities, for your city and for your country, as the Bible encourages us to do.

And when, during the day, anxiety comes over you about what you cannot change, remember that there are things that are yours and things that are God's. You carry out today's task with faithfulness and good cheer. The rest, hand over. The one who sustains kingdoms also knows how to sustain your life, and he does not err in his timing.

o: Lord Jesus, at nightfall, I want to give You thanks for this day. Thank You for the strength You gave me to complete my tasks, for the food that did not run short and for every gesture of kindness I received. Even in the moments when I felt tired or sad, You were near, and today I acknowledge it with a grateful heart. Today, Lord, I feel at peace because of Your care.

You are the one who sees the tears of those who suffer and has compassion on them. I present to You all who wept in silence today: those who lost a loved one, those facing an illness, those who feel an emptiness that nothing fills. Touch their lives with Your consolation, as You touched that mother's in Nain. And if I myself carry some sorrow, I give it to You now, for You know how to care for it better than I.

Forgive me for what I did wrong and for what I failed to do. Take from my mind fears and rushing, and grant me quiet sleep. May I wake tomorrow with renewed hope, knowing that Your word has the power to raise what seems lost. I rest in Your care, Lord. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Soon after healing a centurion's servant, Jesus went to a town called Nain. His disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he approached the gate of the town, they met a funeral procession: a young man was being carried out for burial, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. With many people from the town, the woman accompanied the coffin.

Think about what this meant. This woman had already lost her husband, and now she was losing her only son. In those days, a widow without children was left utterly helpless. No one had asked anything of Jesus; she had neither cried out nor pleaded. But the Bible says that, when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her: “Do not weep.” Luke tells us that his heart was moved at that very moment.

Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. Jesus said: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: “God has visited his people!” The news spread throughout all Judea and the surrounding country.

This account shows us the heart of Jesus. He does not wait for us to ask him before he sees our pain; he looks at the person, not only the problem. His words “Do not weep” were not a cold command, but the promise of one who has the power to turn sorrow into joy. Even if not all our losses are resolved immediately, his compassion is the same, and his word remains stronger than death.
t.c: Thank you for this day lived. Lay your sorrows on the pillow and let God's tenderness cover them, for he never tires of caring for you. Rest in peace; when you wake, his mercy will already be waiting for you with the morning light.
m: At the end of the day, it is normal for weariness to mix with sadness. Perhaps today you carried a sorrow you have told no one, or a worry that gave you no rest. The widow of Nain walked in silence behind her son's coffin, and Jesus noticed her. This is good news for tonight: your pain does not escape the Lord.

Notice that Jesus first had compassion, then acted. Before speaking with power, he looked with tenderness. This is how he treats those who seek him, and also those who do not yet dare to ask him anything. You can come before him tonight just as you are, without fine words, with your tears and your questions, and he will listen to you with the same compassion.

The book of Proverbs offers us a promise for bedtime: when you lie down, you will not be afraid; your sleep will be sweet. God wants you to rest, not to spend the night turning over in your head what you cannot resolve. Today you can practice something simple: before lying down, name in prayer the sorrows of the day, one by one, and after each, say: “Lord, I leave it in your hands.”

And if you know someone going through grief or sadness, think of a way to accompany them tomorrow. A call, a visit or a brief message can be, like the words of Jesus, a sign of consolation. In this way, the compassion you receive from God becomes compassion for others as well.
